## Report

The claim is well supported by the strongest available evidence and is **not false**. The pivotal MAP.3 (NCIC CTG) trial randomized 4,560 postmenopausal women at elevated risk for breast cancer to exemestane 25 mg/day or placebo. At a median follow-up of 35 months, invasive breast cancer occurred in 11 women on exemestane versus 32 on placebo—a statistically significant 65% relative reduction in annual incidence, published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Goss et al., 2011) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/Nejmoa1103507). This result was corroborated by NCI reporting (https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk) and subsequent quality-of-life follow-up analyses confirming the finding while noting modest negative effects on menopause-related symptoms (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4879707/).

Where nuance is warranted is in interpreting the *magnitude and applicability* of benefit, not its existence. The 65% figure is a *relative* risk reduction; the *absolute* reduction was small (roughly 0.9% event rate reduction over ~3 years) because baseline invasive cancer incidence in this population was low. The USPSTF (2019) reviewed this and related aromatase-inhibitor evidence and concluded that for average-risk women, harms (bone loss, fractures, vasomotor and musculoskeletal symptoms) may outweigh benefits, while for women at genuinely elevated risk, net benefit is positive (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction).

**Conclusion:** The evidence—one large, well-conducted randomized controlled trial plus supportive analyses—confirms exemestane reduces invasive breast cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at elevated risk. Skepticism is reasonable only regarding the *size* of absolute benefit and the fact this applies specifically to high-risk (not average-risk) populations, not the existence of the effect itself.
